A_target.statement:
Let $\struct {K, d}$ be a [[Definition:Compact Metric Space|compact metric space]] and $f: K \to \R$ [[Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Spaces)|continuous]].
Then $f$ is [[Definition:Uniformly Continuous|uniformly continuous]].

B_source.statement: To obtain a uniform parameter on a compact set, cover it by local neighbourhoods, extract a [[Definition:Finite Subcover|finite subcover]], and take the minimum of the finitely many local parameters.

substitutions.the local neighbourhoods of the cover: balls on which the function varies by less than half the tolerance
substitutions.the local parameters attached to each: the radii supplied by continuity at each point
substitutions.the minimum over the finite subcover: the uniform parameter valid at every point

derived.finiteness of the subcover: the minimum of the radii is positive rather than an infimum that could vanish
derived.the uniform parameter: one radius working simultaneously at all points

object_map.reformulation: Replace a pointwise choice of parameter by a minimum over a finite subcover, which is positive.

validity_conditions: Continuity supplies a radius at each point, but the infimum over all points could be zero, which is exactly the gap that compactness closes.
Halving the radii before covering is needed so that two points within the uniform distance lie in a common enlarged ball of the subcover.
Finiteness is essential: only a finite collection of positive radii is guaranteed to have positive minimum.
proof_plan:
Let $\epsilon > 0$.
For each $x \in K$, by continuity choose $\delta_x > 0$ with:
:$\map d {x, y} < \delta_x \implies \size {\map f x - \map f y} < \dfrac \epsilon 2$

By [[Definition:Compact Metric Space|compactness]], finitely many $\map {B_{\delta_{x_i} / 2} } {x_i}$ cover $K$.
Let $\delta = \displaystyle \min_i \frac {\delta_{x_i} } 2 > 0$.

Let $\map d {y, z} < \delta$.
Choose $i$ with $y \in \map {B_{\delta_{x_i} / 2} } {x_i}$; then $\map d {z, x_i} < \delta_{x_i}$.
Hence:
:$\size {\map f y - \map f z} \le \size {\map f y - \map f {x_i} } + \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f z} < \epsilon$
which is the [[Heine-Cantor Theorem]].
{{qed}}
